source: Tax Foundation, State Individual Income Tax Rates and Brackets, 2026 (state revenue departments). States flagged approximate model a simplified schedule; see notes.

AK.name: Alaska
AK.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.

AL.name: Alabama
AL.notes: Checked against the 2025 Form 40 booklet. Pensions from defined benefit plans (federal, state, military and employer plans under IRC 414(j)) are left out; IRA and 401(k) distributions are taxed. Social Security is not taxed. The standard deduction here is the amount for lower incomes combined with the personal exemption ($3,000 + $1,500 single; $8,500 + $3,000 joint). The booklet's table cuts it from AGI $26,000 to $35,500 (to $2,500 single and $5,000 joint); the data follows that as a straight line (std_phase_down).

AR.name: Arkansas
AR.notes: Top rate is 3.7% (H.B. 1001, retroactive to Jan 1, 2026). Bracket widths use 2025 amounts; the Department of Finance's 2026 widths are not confirmed here. Arkansas excludes up to $6,000 of pension and retirement income per person. The cap is counted for every adult of that age, which may overstate it when one spouse has all the retirement income. Military retired pay is exempt (Act 141 of 2017) and uses up the $6,000 retirement exemption.

AZ.name: Arizona
AZ.notes: Arizona's standard deduction follows the federal amount (its filing thresholds in the 2025 Form 140 instructions are the federal $15,750 / $31,500). The deduction amounts themselves were not printed in the text we could read.

CO.name: Colorado
CO.notes: Checked against the 2025 DR 0104 booklet and DR 0104AD. Social Security: a person 65 or older leaves all of it out; at 55 to 64 all of it if federal AGI is $75,000 or less (single) / $95,000 or less (joint), otherwise up to $20,000. Pension, annuity and IRA income: up to $24,000 a person at 65 or older and $20,000 at 55 to 64, less the Social Security subtracted. Benefits are split evenly between spouses, and the pension caps are pooled across the household, which can differ slightly from the form. Retirees 54 or younger subtract up to $15,000 of military retirement pay each; from 55 it falls under the pension subtraction.

CT.name: Connecticut
CT.notes: Connecticut follows the CT-1040 Tax Calculation Schedule (Tables A to E: personal exemption, 2% add-back, recapture and personal tax credit by CT AGI) as printed in the 2024 form (CT-1040 TCS Rev. 12/24); the thresholds are set in law and are not indexed, and no 2026 schedule is published yet. Assumed: the personal tax credit is 100% at or below the first row of Table E. Check against the 2026 form when it appears. Connecticut leaves Social Security out when AGI is at or below $75,000 (single) / $100,000 (joint). The $75,000 / $100,000 thresholds are checked against the 2025 CT-1040 instructions (Line 41, Rev. 12/25). Above the line, the 2025 Social Security Benefit Adjustment Worksheet leaves only 25% of the lesser of total benefits and line 9 of the federal worksheet in income, and that is modelled; line 9 is estimated without tax-exempt interest or adjustments.

DC.name: District of Columbia
DC.notes: Checked against the 2025 D-40 booklet: the rate schedule matches, Social Security is subtracted, and there is no general pension exclusion (only government survivor benefits at 62 and a disability exclusion).

DE.name: Delaware
DE.notes: Personal credit $110 per filer. Delaware excludes up to $12,500 of pension and retirement income per person aged 60 or more. The cap is counted for every adult of that age, which may overstate it when one spouse has all the retirement income. Under 60, a military pension exclusion of up to $12,500; from 60 it falls under the pension exclusion.

FL.name: Florida
FL.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.

GA.name: Georgia
GA.notes: Georgia excludes up to $35,000 of retirement income per person aged 62 to 64 and $65,000 at 65 or more. The cap is counted for every adult of that age, which may overstate it when one spouse has all the retirement income. Retirees under 62 exclude up to $17,500 of military retirement income, or $35,000 for those with more than $17,500 of their own earned income; from 62 it falls under the retirement exclusion.

HI.name: Hawaii
HI.notes: Standard deduction plus personal exemption combined. Checked against the 2025 N-11 instructions: distributions from employer-funded pension plans are exempt; IRA and 401(k) withdrawals are treated as taxable here.

IA.name: Iowa
IA.notes: Iowa exempts retirement income for anyone 55 or older (2023 law).

ID.name: Idaho
ID.notes: Idaho conforms to federal law, so its standard deduction matches the federal amount (Idaho Tax Commission, What's new for 2025 returns). The 2025 rate is 5.3% above a zero bracket of $4,811 (single) / $9,622 (joint), which is not modelled; the zero bracket is close to the amount the standard deduction replaces. The enhanced senior deduction is not modelled. Military retired pay is deducted from age 62 up to $48,216 (single) / $72,324 (joint), less Social Security received (Form 39R line 8); the CSRS, Idaho police and firefighter pensions that share the deduction, and the disability route at any age, are not modelled.

IL.name: Illinois
IL.notes: Illinois exempts retirement income from qualified plans, IRAs and pensions entirely (35 ILCS 5/203(a)(2)(F)). Checked against the 2025 IL-1040 instructions: the personal exemption is $2,850 per person ($5,700 joint), used here as the deduction. Not modelled: $1,000 more for each filer 65 or older or blind, and no exemption when federal AGI is over $250,000 (single) / $500,000 (joint).

KS.name: Kansas
KS.notes: Standard deduction plus personal exemption combined. Kansas exempts KPERS, federal civil service and military retirement; enter those as a government pension. Other pensions and IRA withdrawals are taxed.

KY.name: Kentucky
KY.notes: Kentucky excludes up to $31,110 of pension and retirement account income per person. The cap is counted for every adult of that age, which may overstate it when one spouse has all the retirement income. Checked against the 2025 Form 740 packet: standard deduction $3,270 (2025; the 2026 figure is not yet published). Joint filers get one deduction here, which may overstate tax slightly. The 2025 rate is 4%; the 2026 rate of 3.5% is kept from the earlier check.

LA.name: Louisiana
LA.notes: Louisiana exempts up to $12,000 of pension, annuity and IRA distributions for each person 65 or older (IT-540 instructions, code 06E). Federal, state and teacher retirement benefits are fully exempt in Louisiana; enter them as a government pension.

MA.name: Massachusetts
MA.notes: 5% plus 4% surtax over $1M; the $4,400 ($8,800 joint) personal exemption stands in for the standard deduction.

MD.name: Maryland
MD.notes: Standard deduction and rate schedule match the Comptroller Tax Alert on the 2025 legislative session (rev. Dec 22, 2025): flat $3,350 single / $6,700 joint plus the $3,200 exemption per person, with new 6.25% and 6.5% top brackets. Not modelled: exemption phase-out at higher incomes; county income tax is not included. Pension exclusion (Worksheet 13A, 2025): up to $41,200 of employer plan pension and annuity income per person 65 or older, less the Social Security and railroad retirement benefits received. IRA withdrawals do not qualify, so only pension streams are counted; all benefits are deducted from the ceiling even when only one spouse has a pension. Disability, military and public safety exclusions are not modelled. Military retirement income: up to $12,500 under 55 and $20,000 from 55, each.

ME.name: Maine
ME.notes: Checked against the 2025 Form 1040ME instructions and Schedule 1S. Social Security is not taxed. Each person 55 or older may deduct up to $48,216 of pension and IRA income, less all Social Security and railroad benefits received; the deduction fades out over $100,000 of AGI above $125,000 (single) / $250,000 (joint). Standard deduction and exemption phase-outs are not modelled.

MI.name: Michigan
MI.notes: Checked against the 2025 MI-1040 booklet, Schedule 1 and Form 4884. The 2025 rate is 4.25% and the exemption $5,800. From 2026 the retirement and pension subtraction phases in to 100% for people born after 1945 and before 1967: up to $65,897 (single) / $131,794 (joint), the 2025 limit (it is indexed each year), less military and railroad benefits. When the older person was born 1946 to 1952 (Tier 2) the $20,000 / $40,000 Michigan Standard Deduction on all income is used instead when larger; for 1953 to 1958 (Tier 3) it is cut by taxable Social Security and the exemptions (Schedule 1 lines 25 and 26, Worksheet 2). Assumed: these choices carry on into 2026. Not modelled: the +$15,000 for Social Security exempt public work, unlimited public pensions for people born before 1946, and their $14,688 / $29,376 interest and dividend subtraction.

MN.name: Minnesota
MN.notes: Standard deduction phase-out at higher incomes is not modelled. The $84,490 / $108,320 thresholds are checked against the Minnesota Department of Revenue's Social Security subtraction page (updated 2025-12-17), which also says the subtraction falls 10% for each $4,000 of AGI over them; House Research (Minnesota Taxation of Social Security, 2025) confirms a part of $4,000 counts as a full step, and that is modelled. A bill to make the subtraction unlimited (H.F. 100) was seen only as a proposal, not as law.

MO.name: Missouri
MO.notes: Checked against the 2025 MO-1040 instructions and Form MO-A. Social Security is left out. Private pension, IRA and 401(k) income is exempt up to $6,000 a person, less every dollar by which AGI (less taxable Social Security) is over $25,000 single / $32,000 joint. Government pensions (federal, state, local) are exempt up to $47,633 a person (the top Social Security benefit), less the Social Security exemption, with no income limit (MO-A Part 3 Section A); enter them as a government pension. The per-person limits and the joint line are applied to the household.

MS.name: Mississippi
MS.notes: Mississippi exempts qualified retirement income (pensions, IRA and 401(k) withdrawals) once the owner is 59 and a half or retired; modelled from age 60.

MT.name: Montana
MT.notes: Follows the federal standard deduction. Checked against the 2025 Form 2 instructions and Schedule I: Montana has no Social Security subtraction (only Tier I railroad benefits, which are not taxed), so the federally taxable amount stays in income. Earlier data assumed a $5,500 / $11,000 deduction.

NC.name: North Carolina
NC.notes: Uniformed services retirement pay is deducted in full (Schedule S line 21; needs 20 years of service or a medical retirement).

NH.name: New Hampshire
NH.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.

NJ.name: New Jersey
NJ.notes: Personal exemption only; no standard deduction. Pension exclusion (nj.gov Retirement Income Exclusions, 2025): age 62 or older, pension, annuity and IRA withdrawals up to $75,000 single / $100,000 joint / $50,000 separate when total income is $100,000 or less, then 37.5/18.75% (single), 50/25% (joint) of them up to $125,000 / $150,000, none above. Total income here is AGI less taxable Social Security. The separate Other Retirement Income Exclusion is not modelled.

NM.name: New Mexico
NM.notes: Checked against the 2025 PIT-1 and PIT-ADJ instructions. Follows the federal standard deduction. Social Security is left out when AGI is $100,000 or less (single) / $150,000 or less (joint, head of household). Each person 65 or older takes an exemption of $8,000 that falls by $1,000 for each step of income (Table 1); the blind exemption, the $30,000 armed forces retirement exemption and the medical expense exemption are not modelled. Up to $30,000 of armed forces retirement pay per retiree is exempt (PIT-ADJ line 24).

NV.name: Nevada
NV.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.

NY.name: New York
NY.notes: Includes the benefit recapture for AGI over $107,650 (IT-201-I 2025 tax computation worksheets). Rates are the 2026 schedule; recapture amounts are derived from them. NYC and Yonkers taxes are not included. New York excludes up to $20,000 of pension and annuity income per person aged 59 and a half or more (modelled from 60). The cap is counted for every adult of that age, which may overstate it when one spouse has all the retirement income. Pensions from New York State, its local governments and the federal government are fully exempt (IT-201-I, line 26); a government pension entered in Golden is treated that way, and pensions from other states' governments should be entered as ordinary pensions.

OH.name: Ohio
OH.notes: Checked against the 2025 IT 1040 booklet. Social Security is left out. Personal exemptions are $2,150 each here (the 2025 amount for income of $40,001 to $80,000; it is $2,400 below and $1,900 above). Retirement income credit (up to $200) and the $50 senior credit apply when income less exemptions is under $100,000; the test here uses income less taxable Social Security. The 2025 top rate of 3.125% over $100,000 and the 2026 flat rate are as in the table.

OK.name: Oklahoma
OK.notes: Standard deduction plus personal exemption combined. Oklahoma excludes up to $10,000 of pension and retirement income per person. The cap is counted for every adult of that age, which may overstate it when one spouse has all the retirement income.

OR.name: Oregon
OR.notes: Personal exemption credit $256 per filer; the federal-tax subtraction is not modelled. Checked against the 2025 Publication OR-17: Social Security is subtracted; the retirement income credit (age 62+, household income under $22,500 / $45,000; 9% of the lesser of retirement income and $7,500 / $15,000 less benefits less income over $15,000 / $30,000) is modelled, with household income taken as federal AGI less taxable Social Security. The federal pension subtraction (by months of service before October 1991) is not modelled.

PA.name: Pennsylvania
PA.notes: Pennsylvania does not tax retirement income (pensions, IRA and 401(k) withdrawals) once the owner has reached retirement age; modelled from age 60.

RI.name: Rhode Island
RI.notes: Checked against the 2025 RI-1040 instructions, Schedule M and the Social Security worksheet. Taxable Social Security is left out for people born on or before March 1, 1959 (age 67 or more in 2026) when federal AGI is under $107,000 (single) / $133,750 (joint); the share of a younger spouse stays in. Up to $50,000 of pension income (not IRA withdrawals) per person born on or before that date is left out under the same AGI limits; the joint figure here assumes both spouses qualify. Standard deduction and exemption phase-outs are not modelled.

SC.name: South Carolina
SC.notes: Same schedule for all filers. South Carolina deducts up to $10,000 of retirement income per person aged 65 or more. The cap is counted for every adult of that age, which may overstate it when one spouse has all the retirement income. Military retirement income is deductible in full and reduces the retirement deduction.

SD.name: South Dakota
SD.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.

TN.name: Tennessee
TN.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.

TX.name: Texas
TX.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.

UT.name: Utah
UT.notes: Checked against the 2025 TC-40 instructions. Social Security stays in income and earns a credit of 4.5% of the taxable benefits, less 2.5% of income over $54,000 (single) / $90,000 (joint). The $450 retirement credit for each person born on or before 1952 (less 2.5% of income over $25,000 single / $32,000 joint) is used instead of the Social Security credit when larger; income is taken as federal AGI. The taxpayer credit is not modelled. The military retirement credit is 4.5% of military retired pay, allowed with the Social Security credit but not with the $450 retirement credit.

VA.name: Virginia
VA.notes: Virginia's age deduction is $12,000 for each person 65 or older, reduced $1 for every $1 that income (AGI less taxable Social Security) is over $50,000 single / $75,000 married (tax.virginia.gov/subtractions). The older rule for people born before 1939 is not modelled. Military benefits subtraction of up to $40,000 each.

VT.name: Vermont
VT.notes: Brackets and standard deduction + exemption from the 2025 IN-111 instructions (2026 widths unpublished). Over $150,000 AGI, tax is at least 3% of AGI (the US-interest subtraction is not modelled). Checked against the 2025 Vermont income booklet (Retirement Income Exemption Worksheet): Social Security is fully exempt under $55,000 (single, head of household, separate) / $70,000 (joint) of Vermont AGI, and the exemption falls in a straight line to nothing at $65,000 / $80,000. The exemption is an either-or with the exemption for some government pensions, which is not modelled. Military retirement pay is exempt in full with AGI up to $125,000, falling to nothing at $175,000 (Military Retirement Income Exemption Worksheet).

WA.name: Washington
WA.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.

WI.name: Wisconsin
WI.notes: Sliding-scale standard deduction is shown at its maximum. From 2025 each person 67 or older may subtract up to $24,000 of retirement income (Publication 126, 1/26); the smaller $5,000 subtraction at 65 for incomes under $15,000 / $30,000 is not modelled. Claiming the subtraction forgoes Wisconsin tax credits, which are not modelled.

WV.name: West Virginia
WV.notes: Checked against the 2025 IT-140 instructions and Schedule M. Each person 65 or older may leave out up to $8,000 of income, less the Social Security left out (Schedule M line 47). For 2025 only 65% of Social Security over $50,000 / $100,000 AGI is deducted; the table here uses the full exemption that applies from 2026. Up to $2,000 a person of West Virginia public employee or federal retirement is left out (Schedule M line 33; enter it as a government pension), and that amount also cuts the $8,000 senior allowance (line 47).

WY.name: Wyoming
WY.notes: No tax on wages or retirement income.
